Paul has spliced them, and the splice is the argument. In Isaiah 28 the stone is a tested cornerstone, a sure foundation, precious. In Isaiah 8 the stone is what the LORD becomes to people who will not take refuge in him — and that passage says he will be a sanctuary and a stone of offence in the same breath.

One stone. Sanctuary and obstacle. The difference is not in the masonry; it is in the approach.

Picture what a foundation stone in a doorway actually does. Come to it as a threshold and it takes your weight and holds you up for the rest of your life. Come at it in the dark, at speed, looking elsewhere, and it takes your feet from under you. The stone has not moved. It is doing exactly what a laid stone does.

And notice that word: laid. God says I am laying it. This was not debris in the road, and it was not a trap set to catch the unwary. It was placed, deliberately, in Zion, at the front of the building, where nobody could get in without meeting it.

Which raises the question the passage will not let you leave vague: what exactly was the offence? Not obscurity — the stone is the most visible thing in the building. The answer is in the shape of the Messiah they were given.

A crucified one. And the difficulty was not merely that it was undignified or disappointing. Deuteronomy 21:23 says that a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God. So a crucified Messiah was not a lowered expectation; it was a contradiction in terms. The one thing the Christ could not possibly be was accursed.

Except that this is precisely what the chapter opened with. At v. 3 Paul wished he could be accursed and cut off for his people, and could not. The stone they tripped over is the one person who could do the thing Paul wanted to do and did it. What made him unthinkable to them is the whole reason he is any use to anybody.

Then the last clause, and it deserves to be read slowly, because after twenty-eight verses of narrowing it is the widest sentence in the chapter. Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.

Count what is not in it. No lineage. No prior standing. No evidence of having been chosen. It is the only sentence in Romans 9 that a frightened reader can act on directly, and Paul has deliberately put it last.

And the word shame is the one Paul used of himself in the opening paragraph of the letter — I am not ashamed of the gospel (1:16). He was not making a brave noise. He was stating what this stone does to the people who trust it: shame is the specific thing it takes away.

So here is a test, and everybody has an answer to it. Name your stone. There is something about Christ that you have to get past rather than merely accept — the exclusivity of him, the wrath in chapter 1, the cross itself, or the requirement to arrive with nothing in your hands after a lifetime of being competent.

Now notice what this verse says about that stone. It was laid. It is not an unfortunate obstruction on the way to God which you must edge around to reach him. It is the foundation. The thing you are stumbling over is not in front of the door. It is the door.

One guard, because the chapter has frightened people and the last verse is where that gets healed or made worse. Whoever means whoever. It is not a trick sentence with a hidden qualifier for those who turn out to have been chosen. Paul, who has just written the most uncompromising paragraph on election in the Bible, ends it by throwing the door open and standing back.

So the chapter that begins with a man weeping ends with a stone and an invitation. In between are Pharaoh and the potter and the vessels and every hard question a reader can ask. And Paul’s final word is not a verdict on anybody. It is an offer with no name on it, addressed to whoever will have it.

God laid a stone in Zion, and the same stone does two entirely different things depending on nothing but what a man does when he reaches it. To those who trip over it, it is the end of the road. To those who fall on it, it is the foundation. It has not changed. It is one stone, in one place, and it has been there since before the foundation of the world.

The builders looked at it, and could not see a use for it, and threw it down the slope. It is holding up everything.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit—<sup>2</sup>that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.<sup>3</sup>For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh.<sup>4</sup>They are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.<sup>5</sup>To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.<sup>6</sup>But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel,<sup>7</sup>and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”<sup>8</sup>This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.<sup>9</sup>For this is what the promise said: “About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son.”<sup>10</sup>And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac,<sup>11</sup>though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls—<sup>12</sup>she was told, “The older will serve the younger.”<sup>13</sup>As it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”<sup>14</sup>What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God’s part? By no means!<sup>15</sup>For he says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.”<sup>16</sup>So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy.<sup>17</sup>For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”<sup>18</sup>So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills.<sup>19</sup>You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?”<sup>20</sup>But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, “Why have you made me like this?”<sup>21</sup>Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use?<sup>22</sup>What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction,<sup>23</sup>in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory—<sup>24</sup>even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?<sup>25</sup>As indeed he says in Hosea, “Those who were not my people I will call ’my people,’ and her who was not beloved I will call ’beloved.’”<sup>26</sup>“And in the very place where it was said to them, ’You are not my people,’ there they will be called ’sons of the living God.’”<sup>27</sup>And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved,<sup>28</sup>for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay.”<sup>29</sup>And as Isaiah predicted, “If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah.”<sup>30</sup>What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith;<sup>31</sup>but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law.<sup>32</sup>Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone,<sup>33</sup>as it is written, “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.”

10.title: Faith Comes by Hearing
10.overview:
Romans 10 moves from the theology of election (chapter 9) to the human experience of faith and the missionary imperative of proclamation. Paul's pastoral heart is again on display: his heart's desire and prayer for Israel is their salvation. Their problem is not a lack of religious commitment but a misdirection of it — a zeal for God that is not according to knowledge, a pursuit of their own righteousness that refuses to submit to the righteousness of God.

The great passage of vv. 9–15 moves from confession and faith to calling on the name of the Lord to preachers sent with good news — a chain that runs from individual conversion back to the sovereign act of apostolic commissioning. The gospel does not reach people automatically; it reaches them through preachers who are sent, who go, who speak. The chapter ends with the sobering testimony of Israel's own scriptures: they have heard, they have understood, and they have not believed. The tragedy of unbelief is complete.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Righteousness for All Who Call: The Nearness of the Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's pastoral longing for Israel's salvation (v. 1) is the emotional key to the chapter. He is not writing as a detached analyst of Israel's religious failure; he is writing as a broken-hearted brother who knows exactly what his people are missing and cannot stop praying for them. The diagnosis is precise: "a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge." Zeal without knowledge is not a small problem; it is perhaps the most dangerous religious condition possible, because it generates confident misdirection.

The contrast between the righteousness of the law and the righteousness of faith (vv. 5–8) draws on Deuteronomy 30, where Moses speaks of God's word as near to the people — not beyond the sea, not in the heights of heaven, but in their mouths and in their hearts. Paul identifies this nearness with the gospel: "the word of faith that we proclaim." The righteousness of God is not a distant achievement to be scaled by heroic effort; it is a near word to be received by confession and faith.

Two verses stand between the diagnosis and that contrast, and the summary above passes over them. They are the hinge of the chapter. Israel, Paul says, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, did not submit to God’s righteousness (v. 3).

Watch the sequence, because it is a clinical description of how a religious life goes wrong. First not knowing what God was offering; then setting about producing a version of it themselves; and finally — the word that makes it a moral matter rather than a misunderstanding — refusing to submit.

That verb is the surprise. One does not expect righteousness to be something a person submits to. But a righteousness that arrives as a gift has to be received on the giver’s terms, and receiving is precisely what a competent, disciplined, self-respecting person finds hardest. The offence of the gospel is not that it asks too much. It is that it will not let you contribute.

Then v. 4, which the summary above never reaches and which the chapter cannot do without: Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. The word is telos, and it carries both senses at once — the terminus and the goal, where a road stops and what it was built to reach.

Both are true here and neither should be dropped. As a route to righteousness the law has come to its end, because the destination has arrived. And it was always heading there; Christ is not an alternative to the law but the thing it was pointing at, which is why Paul can say elsewhere that he does not overthrow the law but upholds it (3:31).

Note also the last clause, because it is the one that opens the door: to everyone who believes. The universal that will ring three times in vv. 11-13 has already sounded here, before the famous verses begin.

Verses 9–13 are among the most frequently memorised in Paul's letters — "If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved." The simplicity is staggering. Two things: confession of lordship, belief in resurrection. Both are the expression of the same faith. And the word "all" rings three times: everyone who believes (v. 11), everyone who calls (v. 13), for he is Lord of all and bestows riches on all who call (v. 12). The gospel has no ethnic or social exclusion clause.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Confession of Lordship

Romans 10:9 makes the confession "Jesus is Lord" (Kyrios Iēsous) the central act of Christian profession. In the first-century Roman world, "Kyrios" was the title of Caesar — the one to whom ultimate allegiance was owed. To confess "Jesus is Lord" was therefore not merely a theological statement but a political one: Jesus, not Caesar, holds ultimate authority over my life. The early church was persecuted not for believing in Jesus but for refusing to say "Caesar is Lord" — because they had already given that title to another. Every true Christian confession has this political dimension: it declares a transfer of ultimate allegiance.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses's vision of the nearness of God's word (Deuteronomy 30) had originally been given to Israel on the plains of Moab, just before they entered the land — as a word of covenant accessibility. God was not hiding Himself; He had given His word and it was near. Paul's application to the gospel makes the same point: the righteousness of God is not a distant achievement but a near word, proclaimed by apostles, received by faith. Now: The simplicity of Romans 10:9 is the permanent rebuke to every complicated scheme of salvation. Salvation does not require a theology degree, a track record of spiritual achievement, or a passage through elaborate ritual. It requires the honest confession of a changed allegiance and the genuine belief in a historical resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The theological argument of chapter 9 has not extinguished Paul’s evangelistic passion — it has intensified it. ’My heart’s desire and prayer’ — election doctrine does not produce fatalism in the apostle; it produces prayer. He prays for Israel’s salvation even while affirming God’s sovereign purpose, because prayer is the God-ordained means through which the God-ordained end is reached. He credits their zeal: it is real, sincere, intense — and precisely because it is misdirected, it is tragic.

Notice first who he is talking to. Brothers — and the church in Rome was by now substantially Gentile. Paul is asking a largely non-Jewish congregation to care about the salvation of Israel, and he does it by opening his own heart rather than by issuing an instruction.

That is not accidental placement. In one chapter he will be warning these same readers not to become arrogant toward the branches that were broken off (11:18). The work of that warning starts here, quietly, with an apostle letting them see what he wants most.

And see where the sentence falls. Chapter 9 ended on a stone laid in Zion and a nation tripping over it. The very next thing Paul does is pray for them. He does not finish the argument and move on to another subject; he finishes the argument and goes to his knees about it.

Which pays off what he began at 9:2-3. There it was grief. Through 9:6-29 it was doctrine — the hardest in the letter. Here it is prayer, and by 11:23 it will be hope. Four movements, one man, no contradiction between any of them.

The phrase is stronger than English usually carries. Heart’s desire is eudokia — good pleasure, delight, the thing you would choose if you could have what you wanted. It is the word used elsewhere of God’s own good pleasure in salvation. Paul’s delight, the thing he would pick above every other outcome available to him, is that these people should be saved.

Not that they should be answered. Not that they should be proved wrong, which was well within his powers and would have been satisfying. Saved.

Then v. 2, and the verb matters: I bear them witness. That is courtroom language, and Paul is appearing for the defence. He is not conceding a point about his opponents. He is testifying to something he knows at first hand.

Because he does know it at first hand. This is the man who described himself as advancing in Judaism beyond many of his own age, extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers; who listed, among his qualifications, as to zeal, a persecutor of the church (Philippians 3:6). When Paul writes about zeal for God that is not according to knowledge, he is not describing a category of person. He is describing himself at thirty.

Which is what keeps the verse from being contempt. He is not a man who never had the disease diagnosing people who do. He is a survivor of it, and he remembers exactly how right it felt.

And that is the thing worth sitting with, because it is genuinely frightening. It is possible to be sincere, disciplined, costly, lifelong and wrong. Israel’s zeal was not a pose; it produced martyrs. Paul’s zeal was not a pose; it produced warrants and a coat held at a stoning. Sincerity is real, and sincerity is not a saving category, and those two sentences have to be held together.

Here is a test that follows from it, and it is more useful than asking whether you are sincere — you already know you are. When did you last change your mind about something in your faith because Scripture required it and not because it suited you?

Ask it seriously. Zeal that is according to knowledge can be corrected, because it is answerable to something outside itself. Zeal that is not according to knowledge has no mechanism for revision; it can only get warmer. If nothing in your convictions has moved in twenty years, that is not necessarily faithfulness. It may only mean nothing has been allowed to speak.

One guard, because this verse gets used as a weapon. Paul is not saying that sincere people of other convictions are simply stupid, and nothing here licenses that tone. He credits the zeal, he bears witness to it, and he wants them saved rather than defeated. A Christian who uses v. 2 to feel superior has managed to extract contempt from a verse written in tears.

And the guard runs the other way too. Knowledge without zeal is not the remedy being proposed. Paul is not recommending cool accuracy over hot error; the chapter that diagnoses misdirected passion was written by a man whose heart’s desire is at the front of the sentence. The cure for zeal without knowledge has never been knowledge without zeal.

Remember, finally, how his own case was resolved. Nobody argued him out of it. He was not shown a better system or persuaded that he had been over-committed. He was stopped on a road and shown, in person, whom he had been so zealous against — and the first thing he asked was who it was he had been fighting. Zeal without knowledge is not cured by having less zeal. It is cured by being introduced to the one you were serving so badly.

verseByVerse.quote: For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
’Seeking to establish their own’ righteousness — not in a crudely self-righteous way, but in the sincere belief that Torah-observance constituted the righteousness God required. The error is theological: ignorance of the righteousness that God gives (as opposed to the righteousness that humans achieve). Christ is ’the end of the law for righteousness’ — telos, meaning both termination and goal: the law always pointed toward Christ as its destination, and in Christ’s coming, the law’s role as the path to righteousness reaches its appointed conclusion.

Take the three verbs of v. 3 in order, because Paul has built a diagnosis and the sequence is the point. They were ignorant. They set about establishing. They did not submit.

Ignorant is the mildest of the three and the most surprising, because these were not people who had neglected the subject. They were the most literate religious community in the ancient world, and they had the oracles of God (3:2). The word is not about stupidity; it is about failing to recognise something that was in front of them.

Then establish, which is a builder’s word — to set up, to erect, to make something stand. And hold it against the verb at the end of the sentence, submit, which means to place yourself underneath. Those are two entirely different physical actions, and the whole verse turns on the difference.

One is a man putting up a structure with his own name on it. The other is a man getting under something somebody else built. You cannot do both at once, and it is not chiefly a failure of understanding that stops a person doing the second. It is that he has spent thirty years on the first and it is nearly finished.

Which is why the verse describes something better than villainy. Picture the man Paul actually has in mind. He tithes. He has never been unfaithful to his wife. He looks after his mother, keeps his word, gives to people in need, and has not missed a service in eleven years — and every bit of that is genuinely good.

Ask him what stands between him and God and he will not sneer at grace or deny that he needs mercy. He will simply begin, somewhere in his answer, to describe himself. That is what establishing your own righteousness looks like from inside. It does not feel like arrogance. It feels like diligence.

Then v. 4, and it is worth having the word exactly. Telos can mean the point at which a thing stops and the point it was aiming at, and English forces a choice the Greek does not. Both are true here, and dropping either one produces an error the church has repeatedly made.

The picture that holds both is a finishing tape. It ends the race — nobody runs on past it — and it is also the entire reason the race was run. It is not the opposite of the track. It is what the track was for.

So the law is not being repudiated. Everything it required has been met, in a person, and the road it laid out has arrived where it was going. Paul has already ruled out the other reading in as many words: do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means; we uphold the law (3:31).

And notice the qualifier that keeps this from becoming lawlessness: Christ is the end of the law for righteousness. It is the law’s role as the route to a right standing that has ended, not the law as God’s word or its power to show you what you are. Nobody is being told to stop reading Leviticus. They are being told to stop trying to climb it.

Now turn it over, because for a certain kind of reader this is the best sentence in the chapter. If Christ is the terminus, then the project is not merely unnecessary. It is over. There is nothing left to establish, and the only thing you can still do with a completed building is put down the tools.

That is a harder instruction than it sounds, because a man who has been building for decades does not know what to do with his hands. The exhaustion of religious people is very rarely caused by their sins. It is caused by a construction project that God ended a long time ago and nobody told them.

Here is a test, and it is quicker than an examination of your motives. Finish this sentence without thinking too hard: I would say I have had a good week with God if I had ______.

Most of us can complete it instantly, and the answer is almost always a list of activities — prayed more, read more, been more patient, not lost my temper on Wednesday. Now notice what that list is. It is a set of scaffolding poles. It is the honest, unembarrassed shape of a man still establishing, and it survives in people whose doctrine of grace is entirely correct.

One guard before leaving it. None of this makes the week irrelevant, and Paul is about to spend chapters 12 to 15 on how to live. What has changed is what the week is for. It is no longer material for a structure; it is the response of somebody who has been housed.

The tragedy of v. 3 is not that Israel wanted righteousness too little. It is that they wanted it enough to spend a nation’s entire history building one — and God was holding out a finished one the whole time, and taking it would have meant putting theirs down.

verseByVerse.quote: For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them. But the righteousness based on faith says, "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?'" (that is, to bring Christ down)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul sets two voices against each other: Moses describing the righteousness of law (Leviticus 18:5 — do and live) and the same Deuteronomy 30 (vv. 12–14) reread through the lens of Christ as the righteousness of faith. The faith-righteousness does not require impossible ascent or descent — Christ has already come down (incarnation) and descended to the dead (death/resurrection). The work that faith’s righteousness requires of us is not cosmic achievement but reception of what God has already done.

Take the Leviticus quotation straight before doing anything with it, because Paul is not accusing Moses of a trick. The person who does the commandments shall live by them is a genuine offer, and it means exactly what it says.

That is worth insisting on. The law is not a trap laid to make people fail. It states terms — do, and live — and the terms are honourable. Paul quotes the same verse for the same purpose when writing to the Galatians (Galatians 3:12). The difficulty was never the offer. It was the doer.

Then notice whom Paul sets against Moses, because it is not himself. Both quotations in this paragraph come from Moses. Leviticus 18:5 is Moses. Deuteronomy 30 is Moses. The contrast is not apostle versus lawgiver; it is the lawgiver stating the terms, and the same lawgiver describing a word that arrives near without anyone having to go and get it.

And Paul is not raiding Deuteronomy out of context, which is the usual charge. Look at where chapter 30 stands. It comes after the covenant curses of chapter 28, after the exile has been described in advance, and immediately after God promises to circumcise the heart of his people so that they will love him and live (Deuteronomy 30:6).

So the nearness Moses speaks of belongs to a passage about restoration after failure and about surgery performed by God on the human heart. It was never a description of an easy law. Paul is reading Deuteronomy 30 where Deuteronomy 30 actually sits.

Then the phrase that opens the quotation, and it repays slowing down: do not say in your heart. Not do not say. Moses uses that formula elsewhere for the sentence a man never speaks aloud — do not say in your heart, my power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth (Deuteronomy 8:17).

It is a warning aimed at private thoughts, which means the thing being forbidden here is not a doctrinal position anybody would defend in public. It is an interior sentence.

So it is worth asking what that sentence sounds like now, because almost nobody says who will ascend into heaven? in those words. Its modern form is short and most Christians have said it this month: there must be something more I have to do.

That is the ascent. It is the reflex that hears the gospel, believes it in principle, and then quietly sets about assembling a ladder — more discipline, more feeling, a better run of weeks — as though Christ needed fetching down and the fetching were your job.

And Paul’s answer is not that the climb is difficult. It is that the climb is unnecessary, because the journey has already been made in the opposite direction. Nobody has to bring Christ down. He came down. The ladder is not too short. There is nothing at the top of it that is not already standing beside you.

verseByVerse.quote: "or 'Who will descend into the abyss?'" (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart" (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);
verseByVerse.commentary:
The inaccessible has been made accessible: the word of faith is ’near’ — in the mouth, in the heart. Paul’s appropriation of Deuteronomy 30 is typologically rich: the same nearness that Moses promised about the law (it is not too hard, not too far away) now characterizes the gospel. The word of faith that the apostles proclaim is not located in heaven (requiring an ascent to find it) or in the abyss (requiring a descent to retrieve it) — it is present, immediate, preached, available. The only requirement is to hear and believe.

One honest observation first, because Paul has done something to the text and it is better named than glossed. Deuteronomy 30:13 does not say abyss. It says beyond the sea — who will go over the sea for us and bring it to us?

Paul has changed it, deliberately, to the realm of the dead. That is not carelessness or a faulty memory; it is interpretation of exactly the kind Jewish teachers of his day practised openly, and he signals it each time with that is. He is telling you he is applying the passage, not reciting it.

And the substitution is doing real work. Over the sea is merely far. The abyss is the place from which nobody returns — and that is the second of the only two directions a human being could travel to reach God. Up, and down. Paul closes both, because Christ has now been to both and come back from both.

Which gives the other interior sentence, the one v. 7 is aimed at. If the ascent is there must be something more I have to do, the descent is its opposite and it is spoken by a different kind of reader: what he did cannot reach as far down as I have gone.

That sentence has kept more people from Christ than atheism ever has. It does not deny the gospel. It simply holds that this particular case is beneath its range — the thing done at nineteen, the years nobody knows about, the marriage wrecked on purpose. And Paul answers it by pointing at where Christ has been.

Then v. 8, and the word to sit with is near. Not available. Not obtainable. Near — and then located with startling precision: in your mouth and in your heart.

Measure that against where people instinctively put it. Nearer than the church building. Nearer than the minister. Nearer than the next conference, the next book, the next season when things have calmed down enough to think properly. The gospel is not somewhere you must get to. On Paul’s account it is already in the room, and closer than the furniture.

But notice the last clause, because it stops this becoming mysticism: the word of faith that we proclaim. The word did not become near by drifting. It got near because somebody said it out loud.

That is not a small point and Paul is about to build six verses on it — how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard (v. 14)? The nearness of v. 8 and the preacher of v. 15 are the same fact seen from the two ends.

Here is a test the passage hands you ready-made. Name the thing you privately believe still has to happen before you are right with God. Everyone has one, and most people can produce it in under ten seconds.

Now notice which direction it points. Either it is something more you must achieve, which is the ascent — or it is something too far gone to be reached, which is the descent. There is no third option, and Paul has named and closed both of them before he gets to v. 9.

One guard, so nearness is not mistaken for possession. The word being near is not the same as the word being received; that is precisely why the next verse asks for confession and belief. A thing can be in your mouth because you were taught it as a child and never once believed it.

And a guard the other way. In your heart does not mean the word is your own inner voice, or that you should look inside yourself to find it. It is near because it was brought and spoken, from outside, by someone sent. What is inside you is where it has landed, not where it came from.

The two questions of vv. 6 and 7 are the only two a person can ask, and both are questions about travel. Who will go up. Who will go down. Paul’s answer is that the travelling is finished, and that the whole distance a sinner now stands from God is the width of an open mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved. — Romans 10:9–10
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two elements — confession and belief — are not sequential steps but two aspects of the same faith. Believing in the resurrection is the content of saving faith: the conviction that Jesus of Nazareth, crucified under Pontius Pilate, was raised bodily from the dead by God and vindicated as the Lord of all. Confessing Jesus as Lord is the public declaration of that faith’s personal implications: He is Lord over my life, my allegiances, my future.

Believe in your heart — not merely mental assent but the deep personal trust of the whole person. The heart in biblical usage is the seat of the will, the affections, and the personality — the centre of the person. Saving faith is not a thought held in the mind; it is a conviction lodged in the deepest part of the person that reorients everything else. As Calvin defined it: knowledge of God’s grace, firm and certain, rooted in the promises of Christ, revealed by the Holy Spirit.

Two words carried the whole confession in Greek: Kyrios Iēsous. It is worth knowing what those two words cost. Pliny, the governor of Bithynia, wrote to the Emperor Trajan around the year 112 to ask what should be done with Christians, and described the test he had settled on. They were brought in, offered incense and wine before the emperor’s image, and asked to curse Christ. Those who did were released. An entire capital examination came down to one sentence, said where witnesses could hear it.

That is why the mouth is named. Not because God needs to hear the syllables — he has already read the heart — but because the mouth is the organ that costs. Kyrios was Caesar’s own title, the word for the one who held the final right over your life. To hand it to a crucified Galilean was to take it off somebody else. The early Christians were not killed for what they believed; the empire was largely indifferent to private opinion. They were killed for what they would not say. Confession is a transfer of allegiance, and Paul will do something more startling still with that title four verses on.

Which is why this verse is not a password, and that has to be said plainly, because it is used as one. Jesus blocked the magical reading before Paul ever wrote the sentence: Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 7:21) — the exact words of the confession, on lips he does not know. Nothing is saved by the sound. Paul’s own comment elsewhere is that no one can say Jesus is Lord except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). The confession is not what causes the new life. It is the first noise the new life makes.

Then comes the verse the famous one is usually quoted without: For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved (v. 10). The order has reversed. Verse 9 said mouth and then heart; verse 10 says heart and then mouth. Paul is not being careless. In verse 9 he is still walking through Moses’s sentence in Moses’s order — the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart (v. 8, quoting Deuteronomy 30:14) — taking the two organs as the text handed them to him. By verse 10 the quotation is behind him, and he sets them down in the order in which they actually happen.

So these are not two requirements to be assembled, and neither is a stage the other has to wait for. It is one faith described twice: once from the inside, where it is trust, and once from the outside, where it is audible. Nor are justified and saved two different prizes, a smaller one for believing and a better one for speaking. They are one rescue named twice — once by what it does to your standing at the bench, once by what it does to your future.

You will be saved is a future tense and should be left future; there is a day it is pointing at. But the verdict is not deferred with it. That has already been handed down.

All of which matters enormously to one particular reader: the one who has gone back over their life looking for the moment when they confessed properly, and cannot find it. Someone converted alone in a hospital bay with nobody in the room. Someone who came to faith so gradually there is no date to write down. Someone who cannot speak at all. Look at the verb. With the mouth one confesses is a present tense, and it is a description, not a ceremony — not an event you may have failed to perform, but what a believer’s mouth goes on doing.

The word is homologeō, to say the same thing: to agree with God about his Son, where it can be heard. You have done it every time you have prayed to him, every time you have called him Lord in a room where that was awkward, every time you told the truth about whose you are when a shorter answer was available. The verse is not asking whether there was a moment. It is asking whether there is a mouth that agrees with the heart.

Here is a test, and it does not require you to audit your past. Think of the last time you had a plain opportunity to say whose you are and let it go by — and then notice what you were actually afraid of. Not hell, not the loss of your soul. Something far smaller: a change in somebody’s expression, a conversation turning heavy, a reputation for being that sort of person. That fear is a very small piece of the thing that made this sentence dangerous in Rome, and the verse names the mouth on purpose, because that is the fear it is answering.

And why the resurrection, of everything that might have been named as the content of faith? Because you cannot call a dead man Lord. Kyrios is a title for someone currently in office. The raising is God’s own verdict on the crucifixion — the Son declared to be the Son of God in power by it (1:4), and raised for our justification (4:25). Verse 10 says that believing is unto righteousness; chapter 4 said the raising was for our righteousness. The event you are asked to believe and the ground on which you are declared right are the same event.

One last thing, and it runs the length of the letter. The argument reached its lowest point in chapter 3 with a courtroom gone silent — the law speaks so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may be held accountable to God (3:19). That is where this letter left the human mouth: shut, with nothing left to plead. Seven chapters later the first thing the gospel does with a stopped mouth is give it something to say. And what it is given to say is not a defence. It is a name.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Scripture says, "Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame." For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who believes — the universality is the point. The same text (Isaiah 28:16) that Paul cited in 9:33 is cited again: everyone admits no ethnic, cultural, or social distinction. No distinction between Jew and Greek — the covenantal priority of Israel (1:16, to the Jew first) does not mean a different method of salvation. There is one Lord for all, one way of salvation for all, one inexhaustible generosity for all who call on him. The riches he bestows — justification, peace, the Spirit, adoption, hope — are available to every caller without limitation.

That the universality is the point can be shown, not merely asserted, and the evidence is sitting in plain view. Paul quoted this identical sentence fourteen verses ago, at the close of chapter 9, and it did not have the word everyone in it. Isaiah does not have it. The Greek Old Testament Paul was reading does not have it. He put it there. The one word he adds to the prophet is the word this whole paragraph is built on, and he will say it twice more before the paragraph ends.

Which is worth pausing over, because everyone is an easy word to believe in general and an almost impossible one to believe in particular. Nobody disputes it as a doctrine. Almost everybody keeps a private exceptions clause. Sometimes the exception is another person — a case so long-running and so obviously closed that hoping has begun to feel like poor judgement. Sometimes, more quietly, the exception is oneself.

Here is how to find out which you are holding, and it can be done tonight. Do not ask yourself whether you believe the word everyone; you will say yes. Listen instead to how you pray for the person whose case you have privately filed as hopeless. Are you praying as though the promise covers them, or as though you were applying for an exception to be made? The two prayers sound quite different, and you can hear which one is yours. Paul has already modelled the first sort at the top of this chapter: his heart’s desire and prayer to God for people who had rejected the gospel is that they may be saved.

Then verse 12, and the three words that open it are the same three Paul used in chapter 3: there is no distinction. He wrote them once before, at 3:22, and there they introduced the worst news in the letter — there is no distinction: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. The phrase was a leveller. It swept away every advantage anybody had ever counted on and left the whole world standing on one floor.

Here he picks up the same phrase and turns it the other way round. The words that closed every door are the words that now open one. Nobody is far enough in to be exempt from needing this, and nobody is far enough out to be barred from having it — and it is the same sentence doing both jobs. That is not a coincidence of vocabulary; it is the shape of the argument. The gospel can be for everybody only because the ruin was.

And notice the ground Paul actually gives for it, because it is not sentiment about inclusion. It is monotheism: the same Lord is Lord of all. If there were two Lords there could be two ways. There are not. One Lord means one door, and it also means that a Gentile calling on Jesus is not being admitted to somebody else’s God as a guest. He is calling on his own Maker.

The last phrase deserves its verb. Bestowing his riches is a present participle — being rich toward all who call on him — and it does not describe a fixed sum being divided among claimants. This matters to a particular reader: the one who came late, or came out of a wasted stretch of years, and carries the settled impression that whatever is left for them will be the reduced portion. There is no reduced portion. Nobody arriving now is being served what earlier arrivals did not finish.

Which leaves exactly one distinction standing in the paragraph, and it is not the one anybody was arguing about. Not Jew and Greek, not early and late, not the respectable and the wreckage. Only this: those who call on him, and those who do not. And that is not a line anybody is born on the wrong side of.

verseByVerse.quote: For "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joel 2:32 — a text about Israel’s eschatological restoration — is applied universally. Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. The word everyone (pas) appears three times in this short passage (vv. 11, 12, 13) — Paul is hammering the universality of the gospel’s offer. The method of salvation is calling on the name of the Lord: not ritual, not ethnicity, not achievement, but the cry of the soul that reaches out to the sovereign God who saves. Acts 2:21 places this verse at the founding moment of the church’s Pentecost proclamation.

But the largest thing in this verse is the thing it does not stop to explain, and a reader can pass over it a hundred times. Go back to Joel and look at who is being called on. In the Hebrew, the name of the LORD is the name given at the burning bush — four consonants that a synagogue reader would not pronounce, substituting Adonai as he came to them so that the name itself never crossed his lips. That is the name in Joel 2:32. Paul takes that sentence, about that name, and applies it without a word of justification to Jesus of Nazareth.

Consider what has just happened. A man trained as a Pharisee, who had handled the sacred name with that much care his whole life, hands it to a Galilean executed outside Jerusalem within his own adult lifetime — and does it in a subordinate clause, introduced by for, as a proof of something else. He is not arguing that Jesus is divine. He is reasoning from it. This is the highest claim in the chapter and it is made in the quietest sentence in it.

He has been laying the ground for four verses, which is why he can be so brief. Confess that Jesus is Lord (v. 9). The same Lord is Lord of all (v. 12). And now the Scripture that says everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. The title moves from a confession, to a claim about scope, to the covenant name of God, without ever changing hands. It is the same Lord throughout, and by verse 13 it is clear which Lord Paul has meant all along.

Joel is also worth reading for what saved is being saved from, because the promise is not floating. It stands at the end of a passage about the day of the LORD — the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood before that great and awesome day comes. Then: and it shall come to pass that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved. That is rescue with a date and a specified danger. And Romans has named the same danger twice already: the wrath revealed from heaven (1:18), and the day of wrath a hard heart is storing up for itself (2:5). This verse is the exit from that day, and it has one moving part.

Look at how little that moving part requires. Calls — epikaleō — is not a word for eloquence or for correctness. It is what a person does who has no other options left and one name to say. It became, almost immediately, the earliest description of Christians: Paul writes to those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 1:2), and in Damascus the disciples knew Saul was coming for all who call on your name (Acts 9:14). The church’s first name for itself was a verb.

The clearest case in the Gospels is a man with nothing else to bring. He is being executed. He has no time left to make amends, no restitution he can offer, no chance of a changed life to point to, and he cannot even get his hands free. What he has is a mouth and a name, and he uses them: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom (Luke 23:42). He is told today. Everything this verse promises was demonstrated once in public on the worst possible candidate, and Paul’s everyone has to be at least that wide.

Two guards, because a verse this open is easily bent. It is not a formula, for the same reason verse 9 was not — the calling is the sound faith makes, not a lever that operates on God, and Scripture is at pains elsewhere to say that lips can produce these words with nothing behind them.

And for the reader on the other side, who has called and felt nothing back and concluded the call did not register: read the verb of the promise again. It is will be saved. It is not will feel saved. What God attaches himself to here is the calling, not the sensation that may or may not accompany it, and many of the calls he has answered were made by people who were sure at the time that they had spoken into an empty room.

So try to remember, not the best prayer you ever prayed, but the shortest one you ever meant. Two or three words, probably, at an hour you would rather not describe. That is the verb in this verse, and it is the whole of what is being asked. In Joel the name was too holy to be pronounced. In Paul it is the one thing a dying man can still get out.

Everyone. Joel wrote it seven hundred years before there was a church, and the Spirit made sure the word was not Israel, and not the worthy, and not those who have made sufficient progress. Everyone who calls. The name that was too holy to be said aloud in the temple has been put within reach of any mouth on earth, in any language, at any hour, without an appointment and without a mediator standing in the way.

The door was made that wide on purpose, and it cost the one who widened it everything he had.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — The Sent Preacher and Israel's Unbelief
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The logic of the gospel creates a missionary chain that runs backwards from salvation to sending: how can anyone call on one in whom they have not believed? How can they believe in one they have not heard? How can they hear without someone preaching? How can anyone preach unless they are sent? Paul quotes Isaiah 52:7 — "How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!" — and the beauty he celebrates is not aesthetic but teleological: the feet that carry the gospel are beautiful because of what they carry and what their arrival means for those who hear.

The rhetorical questions tighten the logic inexorably: sending → preaching → hearing → believing → calling → saved. Remove any link and the chain breaks. This is Paul's theological argument for the absolute necessity of gospel proclamation. The sovereignty of God in election does not make preaching unnecessary; it makes preaching the instrument through which God calls His elect. "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ" (v. 17). The word is the means; the Spirit works through the means; the elect hear and believe. Preach.

The chain does not then run smoothly to its conclusion, and v. 16 is where Paul says so: But they have not all obeyed the gospel. Every link held. They were sent, they preached, Israel heard — and it was not believed. Paul reaches for Isaiah again, and the line he takes is the opening of the fourth Servant Song: Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us? (Isaiah 53:1). It stands immediately before the description of the man despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions. So the unbelief being grieved here is not a late development. It was written into the prophecy of the cross itself: the servant was foretold as one who would not be believed.

The chapter ends with the testimony of Israel's own scriptures against Israel's unbelief. Have they not heard? Yes — all the earth has heard (v. 18). Did they not understand? Yes — Moses had already anticipated a day when Israel would be provoked to jealousy by a foolish nation (v. 19; Deuteronomy 32:21).

And then Isaiah, whom Paul says is so bold as to put it like this: I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me (v. 20; Isaiah 65:1). That is the hardest sentence in the chapter for anyone who assumes that finding God is the reward for looking for him. God turns up among people who were not enquiring, while the people who held the oracles do not come. Israel's rejection is not ignorance; it is disobedience (v. 21) — the stretching out of God's hands to a disobedient and contrary people. The love of God remains; the response of Israel does not.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Necessity of Preaching

Romans 10:14–17 is the most important New Testament text on the theology of preaching. Preaching is not one option among many for communicating the gospel; it is the divinely appointed means by which faith comes. The Spirit of God works through the proclaimed word — the word heard, the word believed — to create the faith that saves. This is why the Reformed tradition has always given preaching the central place in worship: not as a performance or an educational exercise but as the means of grace through which God speaks and through which His people hear. "Faith comes from hearing" — and hearing requires a preacher, and a preacher requires a sending. The missionary imperative is embedded in the very logic of salvation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The "beautiful feet" of Isaiah 52:7 originally referred to the herald who would bring to Jerusalem the news that the exile was over — Babylon had fallen, and God's people were coming home. Paul applies this image to the heralds of the new exodus: those who proclaim that sin, death, and the wrath of God have been overcome in Christ. The gospel is the announcement that the exile from God is over; the journey home has begun. Now: In an age that has substituted social media presence, personal authenticity, and lifestyle witness for the proclamation of the gospel, Romans 10:14–17 is a direct challenge: people are not saved by our online presence or our admirable lives. They are saved by hearing the word of Christ. We must preach — in whatever form that takes in our cultural moment — because faith comes by hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!' — Romans 10:14–15
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chain of questions in vv. 14–15 is the logical backbone of every missionary theology. Each question depends on the previous one; pull any link out and the chain fails. The urgency of sending preachers is therefore not an optional add-on to the Christian life but a structural necessity for the salvation of anyone who has not yet heard. If faith comes by hearing and hearing requires a preacher and a preacher requires sending, then the church that does not send is obstructing the chain at its most upstream link.

Spurgeon used to say that if sinners will be damned, let them at least leap over our bodies to get there — let it not be said that they perished for lack of a warning. The urgency of Romans 10:14–15 is not guilt-driven anxiety; it is the urgency of love, fully aware that the means of salvation is the word faithfully proclaimed.

Notice which way the chain is running, because it is running backwards and that is the whole point of it. Paul has just said that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. So he asks what must already have happened for anybody to be in a position to call — and works upstream, one link at a time, until he arrives somewhere that surprises. The chain does not stop at the preacher. It stops at a passive verb: unless they are sent. Somebody else has to act first.

That passive is where the doctrine of this chapter and the practice of the church are joined. Nobody in this sequence appoints himself, and the sending does not finally originate with a committee. It is God’s own initiative arriving in ordinary shoe leather. Which also settles the objection people raise here — that if God has chosen his people, the preaching is a formality. Paul is arguing the reverse. The same God who appointed the harvest appointed the plough, and no farmer who is certain of a crop therefore leaves the seed in the barn. Election does not make proclamation optional; it is what makes proclamation worth doing, because it guarantees that the word will not come back empty.

This is also where the promise of v. 8 gets paid. The word is near you, Paul said, in your mouth and in your heart. But it did not become near by drifting there. Ask how it got into your mouth and the answer is that it was in somebody else’s first. The nearness of v. 8 and the preacher of v. 15 are not two subjects. They are one fact seen from the two ends.

Then Paul reaches for Isaiah, and the sentence he chooses is worth staging rather than quoting. Isaiah 52 is set in a city waiting for news it has no way of getting. Word travelled at the speed of a man’s legs; the wall had watchmen on it precisely because there was no other way to learn how the war had gone. And what a watchman sees first, as a runner comes over the ridge, is feet — the feet crest the skyline before the man does. How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news (Isaiah 52:7).

Nobody in that world thought feet were beautiful. Feet were the filthiest part of a person, the part a household slave was given to wash. Isaiah calls them lovely anyway, because of what is attached to them further up. And look at what the herald in Isaiah is actually shouting, because it is not a general religious sentiment: peace, good news, salvation, and then the line the whole scene is built for — Your God reigns. The exile is over. The occupying power has fallen. There has been a change of government and you can go home.

Which is the same announcement Paul has been unpacking since v. 9. The herald on the ridge cries Your God reigns; the believer at the bottom of the hill says Jesus is Lord. It is one sentence, shouted from the top and answered from the bottom, and the road between them is the thing Paul is describing in these two verses.

So here is a question that is not rhetorical, and almost everybody can answer it. Who told you? Not who taught you afterwards — who first put the thing into words in your hearing. A parent, a friend at work, a teacher, someone at a door, someone who said it badly and said it anyway. You are standing at the end of a run of feet, and you can usually name the last pair. Then ask the second half of it: who told them?

A guard is needed here, because this passage is regularly used to apply pressure, and pressure is not what it is doing. The verb is passive — unless they are sent — so the chain never asks any individual to manufacture a calling he has not been given, and it plainly needs senders as well as goers. Nor does it make you responsible for the result; the very next verse says outright that faithful preaching and general believing are two different things.

What the passage does establish is that the message must travel, and that people are not saved by the light they already have — as the opening of the letter put it, creation is enough light to leave a man without excuse and not enough to save him. General revelation closes the mouth. Only the gospel opens the door.

There is nothing beautiful about feet. There was almost certainly nothing striking about the person who told you — no eloquence you can remember, possibly an awkward conversation you would not want repeated. That is not where the beauty was. It was in what they were carrying, and it made them lovely all the way down to the dirt on their shoes.

verseByVerse.quote: But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, 'Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?' — Romans 10:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chain of vv. 14–15 establishes the necessity of preaching; v. 16 acknowledges the painful reality that preaching does not guarantee believing. They have not all obeyed the gospel — the word obeyed is significant: faith is not merely intellectual assent but the obedience of the whole person to the message. And not all give this obedience. Isaiah had experienced the same grief: Who has believed what he has heard from us? The prophet who proclaimed the Servant Songs to Israel found that Israel largely did not believe.

This is not a counsel of despair for the preacher; it is a realistic expectation that the faithful messenger has always faced. Not every field produces a harvest at the same rate; not every sermon produces immediate visible fruit. The preacher’s task is faithfulness to the message, not management of the results. Results belong to God. The question Isaiah asked — who has believed? — will have an answer on the last day that surprises both the discouraged preacher and the confident self-assurer.

Weigh the two words Paul chose, because he is being exact and it is easy to read past them. He does not write that Israel has not obeyed. He writes not all. That qualification is load-bearing: it leaves the remnant standing, it is why chapter 11 can open with the question of whether God has rejected his people and answer it with a flat no, and it stops this verse being turned into a verdict on a whole nation.

And notice which word it is. Three times in the last six verses the drumbeat has been everyone — everyone who believes, all who call on him, everyone who calls on the name of the Lord. It is the same Greek word here, turned over. The word that was a promise has become a measurement, and the measurement comes back short. That is the sound of the chapter’s hope meeting the chapter’s grief in a single syllable.

The quotation deserves its address, because the entry above is right that Isaiah knew this grief and the location makes it sharper still. It is Isaiah 53:1 — the opening line of the passage about the servant. The very next sentence is the one about a man with no form or majesty that we should look at him, despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions. So the question who has believed what he has heard from us? is not a general complaint about a hard audience. It is the preface to the report itself, and the report is a crucified man. The difficulty was never that the message was badly delivered. It is what the message says, which is the same thing chapter 9 called a stone people trip over.

Then obeyed, which the entry above rightly flags and which repays another look. News is not normally something you obey. You believe a report or you disbelieve it; nobody obeys a weather forecast. Paul says obeyed because of what this particular news announces. The herald on Isaiah’s ridge two verses ago was shouting that there had been a change of government. An announcement like that does not merely inform you; it puts you under someone. Which is why unbelief in this chapter keeps being described in the language of refusal rather than of error — they did not submit (v. 3), they have not obeyed (v. 16), they are disobedient and contrary (v. 21).

Now the pastoral weight of the verse, which is considerable, because the person most likely to be reading it hard is not a professional preacher. It is a mother who has said it to a son for eleven years. A man whose brother changes the subject. Someone who brought a friend to church twice and has watched the friend go quietly cold on the whole business. They know what verse 16 says before they read it.

To that reader, look at what Isaiah was actually sent to do, because it is more startling than the verse quoted here. When God commissioned him, the commission itself described the outcome: go and say to this people, keep on hearing but do not understand (Isaiah 6:9). Isaiah asked the only question a person could ask — How long, O Lord? — and was told, until the cities lie waste without inhabitant. That is the prophet whose sentence Paul is borrowing. If faithfulness were measured by response, Isaiah failed for a lifetime, and so did Paul with his own people, and the New Testament would have to be rewritten around a different definition of success.

But a guard belongs here, because results belong to God is true and is also the standard alibi of the lazy and the cold. Look at how Isaiah phrases his despair. The version Paul quotes begins by naming an addressee: Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us? It is not a shrug delivered to an audience. It is a grief handed upward. And Paul has already shown the same reflex at the top of this chapter, where his response to his people’s unbelief was to pray for them.

So there is a test, and it is about your own voice. When the person who will not believe comes up, listen to what you say about them when they are not in the room. Is it Isaiah’s sentence, with the word Lord at the front of it and a real ache behind it? Or is it a verdict, delivered to somebody else, about a case you have privately closed? The two can use almost identical words about the same person. Only one of them is still praying.

The chain of the previous verses was not wrong, and this verse does not break it. It simply refuses to let it be read as a machine. Sent, preached, heard — and then a gap that no amount of sending closes, because the last link was never ours to operate. Which is exactly why the next verse goes back to the beginning and names the one thing that does the work.

verseByVerse.quote: So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ. — Romans 10:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
This sentence is the theology of preaching in seven words. Faith is not generated by argument, emotional experience, or social influence — though all of these may play a role. Faith is generated by the word of Christ — the specific, particular, apostolic proclamation of Jesus Christ as Lord and Saviour — when it is heard. The Holy Spirit uses the word as His instrument; the word is the means of grace through which the Spirit creates faith in the hearts of the elect.

This is why expository preaching — the careful, faithful, systematic exposition of what the text of Scripture actually says — has always been central to the Reformed tradition. Not because Reformed people love lectures, but because they believe this verse: it is the word of Christ that creates faith. The preacher’s task is to get out of the way and let the word do its work.

Start with the little word the verse opens on, because most readers cannot account for it. So — Paul is drawing a conclusion, and from what? From the sentence he has just quoted. Isaiah asked, Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us? The Greek noun there is akoē, and it carries both meanings at once: the act of hearing, and the thing that is heard, the report. Paul has taken the prophet’s own noun and drawn the doctrine out of it. If faith is what Isaiah found missing when the report went out, then faith is the thing that comes by the report.

Which is why the verse cannot be flattened into a general recommendation of listening. It is not saying that faith arrives through auditory experience. It is saying that faith arrives through a specific message with a specific content, and Paul names it: the word of Christ. Not a word about God in general, not encouragement, not religious atmosphere. The report is about him, and there is no other report that does this.

Now the practical half, because this verse answers the most common request in the Christian life. Almost everyone has said, in one form or another, that they wish they had more faith. Notice that people who say it are almost always trying to solve it inwardly — by concentrating, by resolving, by attempting to feel more certain than they do. And it does not work, because faith is not a substance you can press harder on. It is a response. Responses need something to respond to.

So the verse hands you a lever that is not your own willpower, and it can be tested backwards. Think of the season when your faith was thickest — not happiest, thickest, when God was most obviously real to you — and then ask what you were doing in the weeks before it. Then do the same with the thinnest stretch you can remember, and ask what had quietly stopped. The answers are rarely mysterious. What is under the word gets thicker; what is away from it gets thinner, and it thins so gradually that the person it is happening to is usually the last to notice.

Two guards. The first is that hearing is necessary and not automatic — the verse immediately before this one exists to say so, since not all who heard obeyed. Chapter 2 made the same point from the other side, that hearers of the law are not the ones justified, and the two kinds of hearing are set out there. Sitting under preaching is not the same as receiving it, and a person can do the first for forty years.

The second guard is for the reader who takes hearing too literally and concludes that this shuts them out. Akoē is about a message reaching a person; it is not a statement about ears. The housebound believer with a Bible open, the deaf believer watching an interpreter, the man reading a page in a prison cell — the word of Christ is arriving, and it does there exactly what it does in a crowded building. What the verse rules out is not a particular medium. It is the idea that faith might come from somewhere other than the message.

And there is one more implication that ought to change how an ordinary Sunday feels. Paul says elsewhere that Christ came and preached peace to you who were far off (Ephesians 2:17) — written to people in Asia Minor who had never been within six hundred miles of him and most of whom were not yet converted when he died. He preached to them. He did it through messengers. So the thing you are listening to next Sunday, imperfectly delivered by a tired man with a cold, is not merely a report about a distant event. It is the risen Christ still speaking to people who were not born when he was crucified. That is why the preacher’s business is to get out of the way. Somebody else is talking.

verseByVerse.quote: But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have, for "Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world." But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, "I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two questions close the chapter: Have they heard? Have they understood? Both answers are yes — which is what makes the rejection culpable rather than excusable. Psalm 19:4 (the proclamation of creation itself reaching all the earth) is applied to the gospel’s proclamation: the word has gone out. And Deuteronomy 32:21 (Moses’s song) shows that even Israel’s jealousy at Gentile salvation was prophesied — God had warned that he would make Israel jealous through a non-nation, which Paul understands as the Gentile church.

Take care over who they are in the first question, because this verse is sometimes made to say something Paul spent his life denying. He is not claiming that every human being on earth has now heard the gospel. He tells the same church, five chapters later, that his ambition is to preach where Christ has not been named, and that whole regions still have not been told (15:20–21). The question here belongs to the argument he is running: it is Israel who cannot plead that the message never reached them. It had been announced in their own synagogues, in their own language, by their own countrymen, for thirty years.

And the text he reaches for is a strange one until you see what he is doing with it. Psalm 19 is about the sky. The heavens declare the glory of God, day pours out speech to day, and there is no language where their voice is not heard — a testimony with no translator and no border, arriving everywhere at once simply because it is overhead. Paul is not proving from a psalm about stars that the gospel has been preached in every village. He is borrowing the psalm’s picture of reach. The announcement has gone out the way daylight goes out.

And that closes a circle from the opening of the letter, where the sky was enough to leave a man without excuse; now the message that could actually save him has travelled the same roads.

Then the second question, and Paul calls his witnesses in order — first Moses, and Isaiah will follow in the next verse. What Moses says has a symmetry the quotation only half shows, and it is worth having whole. In Deuteronomy 32:21 God says: they have made me jealous with what is no god, they have provoked me with their idols; so I will make them jealous with those who are no people, I will provoke them with a foolish nation.

It is measure for measure. Israel provoked God by giving his love to a no-god. God answers by giving his love to a no-people. The Gentiles in this sentence are not the better party being promoted; they are chosen for the role precisely because they are the ones nobody counted — a nothing, to answer a nothing.

Now the detail that makes the second question unanswerable. Deuteronomy 32 is the Song of Moses, and Moses was told to teach it to Israel by heart before they ever crossed into the land, so that it would stand as a witness against them in a future they had not yet lived (Deuteronomy 31:19–21). Israel had been singing this for centuries. The prophecy of their own refusal, and of the outsiders who would be brought in over it, was in their hymnbook. Did Israel not understand? They had it memorised.

But notice what the jealousy is for, because it is easy to hear it as spite and it is the opposite. God does not say he will replace them. He says he will make them jealous — which is only worth doing if you intend to get somebody back. Paul will make this explicit in the next chapter, where his own Gentile ministry is described as a way of making his fellow Jews jealous in order to save some of them (11:11, 14). The instrument is not a punishment. It is a recovery operation conducted in public.

Which puts a question to the ordinary reader that has nothing to do with Israel. Jealousy only works on something that looks worth having. Nobody has ever envied a life that appeared joyless, anxious and duty-bound. So it is fair to ask whether anyone watching you at close range — the people who see the unedited version, at home, when things go wrong — would want what you have. That is not a call to perform contentment; performed contentment provokes nothing but suspicion. It is a call to go and get some, from the word that verse 17 just named, so that there is something there to be envied.

And a guard for the Gentile reader, who is being flattered here by nobody. The terms are no people and a foolish nation. The branch that was grafted in has no grounds for looking down the trunk at the branch that was broken off, which is exactly the warning Paul is about to spend a chapter delivering.

Read the two verses together and the shape is remarkable. Refused by the people he had carried for fifteen hundred years, God’s response was not to withdraw. It was to go and be visibly loved somewhere else, in front of them. That is a very strange thing to do unless you mean to be missed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah is so bold as to say, "I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me." But of Israel he says, "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah 65:1–2 provides the sharpest possible contrast. God was found by those who were not looking (the Gentiles); God held out his hands all day to those who were given every opportunity (Israel). The image of outstretched hands is an image of divine patience, longing, and repeated invitation meeting with repeated refusal. Disobedient and contrary — the prophetic indictment of Israel is not Paul’s invention; it is Israel’s own Scripture. The door has been open all along; the tragedy is the refusal, not the inaccessibility.

Paul’s introduction to the first quotation is not decoration. Isaiah is so bold as to say — the verb means to throw caution aside, to dare something. Paul is telling you that the prophet knew he was saying an outrageous thing, and it is worth asking what the outrage was. Not that God saves Gentiles; Isaiah says that repeatedly. The daring part is the manner of it: I was found by those who did not seek me; I was made manifest to those who did not ask for me. God let himself be found by people who were not looking for him.

Which is, for a certain reader, the best sentence in the chapter. There are people who have read chapter 9 and come away frightened, quietly certain that they are not among the chosen, and the evidence they offer against themselves is nearly always the same: I did not really want this. I came to it late, or badly, or for the wrong reasons. I was not seeking. Verse 20 takes that piece of evidence off the table entirely. Not seeking is the qualification of the people God says he was found by.

Now look at how the two quotations sit in the prophet, because it matters more than it looks. Verse 20 is Isaiah 65:1 and verse 21 is Isaiah 65:2. They are consecutive. Paul did not go hunting through the Scriptures for a counterweight; he simply kept reading, and the sovereign grace and the human refusal were already lying side by side in the same paragraph.

That is the answer to a way of reading chapter 9 that has done real damage. If someone closes the book at the potter and the clay, they end with a God who settles everything over people’s heads and a question nobody is permitted to ask. Two chapters later the same apostle ends his argument with God standing in a doorway with his arms out, and assigns the loss to a people who would not come. The word in verse 21 is stronger than disobedient; it means answering back, contradicting — the very posture chapter 9 said the clay had no standing for, now shown to be exactly what the clay did. Both stand. Paul does not soften either one, and neither should anybody using him.

Then take the picture in verse 21 literally for a moment, because familiarity has worn it smooth. Hold your own arms straight out in front of you and see how long it is before the shoulders start to burn. Two minutes is difficult. All day long, says God, I have held out my hands. It is the posture of appeal and of welcome, and it is not a posture anyone maintains casually. Picture a parent standing in a doorway with their arms open from morning until dark while a child walks past them, again, and again, and does not stop.

The Lord Jesus said the same thing about the same city, and he said it out loud in the street: how often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing (Luke 13:34). Same complaint, same posture, same grief — and the word he ends on is not could not but would not.

Isaiah was not writing about the cross, and it would be dishonest to pretend the verse means that. But a Christian cannot read the sentence without seeing where those hands went in the end. Held out. All day. Outside the walls of the city they were held out to. The thing God says he has been doing figuratively for centuries, he eventually did with nails through his wrists, in public, for six hours.

So here is something to do before you pray tonight, and it takes ten seconds. Notice what you are unconsciously picturing God’s posture to be when you come back after a stretch of neglect. Most people picture folded arms, or a turned back, or at best a cool formal patience. This verse says arms out — and it says it about people who were refusing him at the time it was said. Whatever your face imagines, the text has already described the posture, and it is not the one you are bracing for.
